Core mission
04 · find it, fix it · 3 clicks: find it · fix it · learn and repeat
  • Strip security operations down and it's two jobs.
  • Find it: discover every system we own, detect every attack, and work out which ones matter.
  • Fix it: find who owns it, get the owner's approval, contain it or fix it, and verify it's actually closed. Contain is for an attack; fix is for a weak spot.
  • Then learn: every fix and every incident should make the next find faster. And repeat, every day, at our scale. That's our core mission: find it, and fix it. Next: why each half is hard.

06 · we can't find it in time · 8 clicks: one problem per click, each added to our universe; then our mission
  • We can't find it in time, and here's why at our scale. When our SOC started in 2016 it took in about a terabyte of data a day. Today, seven and a half petabytes: seven thousand five hundred times more.
  • We keep buying companies: eleven acquisitions since 2020, from Expanse to CyberArk and Chronosphere, two still closing. Every one lands systems nobody here knows yet. Those black spots.
  • And the cloud never sits still: eight hundred and seventy-seven million cloud assets across three hundred and sixty cloud orgs, changing all the time.
  • Our own Unit 42 research: almost half of high-risk cloud exposures sit on systems that are new that month.
  • A hundred and fifteen thousand internet-facing addresses, every one a door attackers scan daily.
  • AI tools are a new door: twenty-eight known-exploited flaws in AI products this year.
  • And in all of that, ninety billion events a day boil down to one real incident.
  • So our mission: find it before day zero, or right at it, the moment it's public.

The problem

08 · we can't fix it in time · 5 clicks: speed · velocity · people leave · nobody owns it · our mission
  • Speed: attackers now exploit a new flaw in about five days. In 2018 it was sixty-three. Our fix has to find the owner, build the fix, ship it. The attacker lands while we're still in the middle.
  • Velocity: one in five cloud services changes every month. By the time the fix ships, the system it was for has moved.
  • People leave. Reorgs, new jobs. What they owned is forgotten.
  • And when nobody owns it, nobody fixes it. The fixes pile up.
  • So our mission: every flaw has an owner, and every fix lands instantly, before the attacker does.

Sources: Mandiant time-to-exploit 63 days (2018) → 5 days (2023). Unit 42 Attack Surface Threat Report 2023: >20% of cloud-hosted services change every month (industry-wide). Our fix track's days (owner ~3.5, fix ~8, done ~12): ILLUSTRATIVE (Tan to supply a real time-to-fix). "Fix it instantly" is the mission (Target), not a claim. The galaxy is drawn, not counted.

09 · fix it: what we built · 5 clicks: own · fix · contain · verify · what it got us
  • Here's how we repair that broken track, one step at a time. First, ownership: Triangulum maps every system to its owner automatically, so nothing waits for someone to be found. That's our target: found and owned in minutes.
  • Then the fix itself: where it's safe, auto-remediation applies it in thirty seconds.
  • Where we can't fix it yet, we contain it. Orion, our AI SOC agents, works the alarms; our SOC contains a high-priority attack in about a minute.
  • And because one in five cloud services changes every month, Blackbird is being built to re-test our own systems after every change.
  • Our recent developments: thirty seconds to fix where it's automated, a minute to contain. Measured in seconds, the attacker's five days is off the chart.

The goal

Minus days.

Our goalReady before day 0.Target
10 · minus days · 3 clicks: the attackers' window · our stations before day 0 · day 0
  • Remember the title. This line is time; the orange point is day zero, the moment a flaw goes public. Attackers already work around it: about one in four exploited flaws is hit on or before day zero, and the average time to exploit is just five days.
  • So we move our work to the left of day zero. Every system found and owned, so nothing waits for an owner. Our own weak spots found first, by testing ourselves. And we're ready to fix it, or contain it.
  • Then when the flaw goes public, we fix it or contain it right away. That's minus days. It's our target, not a claim: we're building toward it.

Sources: VulnCheck State of Exploitation 1H-2026 (23.43% of KEVs exploited on or before CVE publication day); Mandiant time-to-exploit 5 days (2023). Minus days definition per CLAUDE.md (a Target; never "fixed before day 0" for a vendor flaw). Station roles: Triangulum = inventory/owner (found + owned 14 min is a Target), Blackbird = AI attack simulation on our own systems (INVESTING), auto-remediation = fix (30 s, Real); Orion = contain; 1 min is the SOC-wide figure (Real), not Orion's; Fix-it tool roles still to confirm with Tan. Two separate studies, shown side by side, never combined: Mandiant's 5 days counts from the patch release, VulnCheck's 23% from publication; the bar's start before day 0 is drawn, not measured. On click 3 only the part after day 0 greys: a fix at day 0 does nothing for the hits before it.

The big picture

How it all connects.

MOSAIC
11 · how it all connects · 6 clicks: find it · into the core · inside the core · fix it · the loop · the foundation
  • Before we go deep, here's the whole thing on one page. On the left, how we find it: Cortex scanners find what's out there, those exposures feed Cobra and Atlas, which work out the attack paths, Blackbird tests them on our own systems, and CyberNova brings in what attackers are using right now.
  • Everything flows into one core. It assesses, enriches, validates, prioritizes and investigates: what actually matters to us.
  • Inside the core, five AI agents, which we're building, work on one loop: Mimir judges the threat, Triangulum checks configuration, Andromeda checks our detection coverage, Libra scores the risk, and Sift works the cases like an analyst.
  • Out the other side, four ways it gets fixed: owners see and fix their own exposure, campaigns retire systemic risk at the root, rapid response acts on anything exploitable right now, and auto-remediation fixes the intolerable on sight.
  • And it loops: Blackbird, which we're building, will re-test every fix, so fixed stays fixed.
  • All of it stands on one foundation: our logging, our automation, and health checks on every source, agent and fix. Now, let's go deep, piece by piece.

12 · deep dive · Cobra + Atlas · 5 clicks: map · rank · trace · investigate · today
  • Everything starts here. Cobra, with Atlas, maps everything we own as one graph: one point one million assets, with their logs and actions, every way in, every path. Live screens, names blurred out. The command center: every way in on the left, the paths an attacker could walk in the middle, what they'd reach on the right.
  • Four hundred and thirty-five thousand attack paths, every one scored by risk, impact times likelihood, so we work the worst first, not the loudest.
  • Open one and you see it end to end: an internet-facing server, the identity it runs as, what that identity owns, and the blast radius at the end. Atlas adds what that host has actually been doing.
  • And when a new flaw drops, we ask Cobra which of our assets it reaches, ranked, in five to fifteen minutes.
  • Today: thirteen hundred choke points, single changes that each close ten or more of the top paths.

Where we areBuiltengine · proof step · console · 11-target practice rangeNext · scored runs, then our own production
15 · deep dive · Blackbird · 5 clicks: target · plan · test · prove · learn
  • Blackbird is how we find our own weak spots first: AI attack simulation, run against our own systems, by us, before an attacker does it for real.
  • It starts with one of our own systems, picked by our team. Today that's our practice range.
  • An AI brain plans: it keeps a map of what it knows and goes after the most valuable lead first. It never touches the system itself.
  • The touching is done by throwaway, sandboxed workers with no credentials. Each runs one action and is gone. The rule: they can add data, never change or delete what's there.
  • And it's designed to report only what it can prove: a proof we can replay, plus a weaker control version of the same test that has to fail. One gap in that step is still being closed.
  • Every run feeds the next. The goal is that it gets measurably better every week. Where we are, honestly: the engine, the proof step, the console and an eleven-target practice range are built. Next is scoring it on that range; our own production comes after it clears the bar. Running nonstop is the goal, not today.

16 · Blackbird results · 5 clicks: every finding · the criticals · one chain · another AI model · 56×
  • Here's what it found. One round of runs on eight of our own internet-facing systems: two hundred and eighty-eight findings. One dot each.
  • A hundred and nine of them rated critical, the most severe level. Plus sixty-four high.
  • And it chains. On this system it took three small flaws, the kind a scanner files as medium and moves on, and linked them into one full account takeover. That's how real attackers work, and now so do we.
  • Same engine, same systems, another strong AI model: the small dots. Five of these systems changed between runs, so we only compare the three that didn't.
  • Fifty-six critical findings against one. Fifty-six times more. The model matters, and attackers will have models like this too. So we point it at ourselves first.

The loop at work · a PHP flaw

One flaw, end to end.

ILLUSTRATIVE SCENARIO
CASE · A CRITICAL PHP FLAW0min
20 · one flaw, end to end · 8 clicks: our SOC sends one kind of agent per click; each goes out, does one job on our systems, comes home, and its report lands in the case log on the left
  • On the right, our SOC and our systems, with the web portal planet at the edge, facing the internet. On the left, the case log: it writes itself as the agents report. Minute zero: CyberNova picks up a critical PHP flaw from the outside world, and attackers are already using it. The warning drops into our SOC, and a case opens.
  • Cobra and Atlas map our whole attack surface and every exposure: two hundred and thirty systems light up. One web portal faces the internet, and from it an attacker could reach two internal systems.
  • Mimir assesses the threat: its hunting agents circle the portal and the two systems behind it. Is anyone already inside? No one. So yes, it matters, and it's not too late.
  • Blackbird proves the exposure: three ships go to our own portal, safely and in scope, and each one finds a hole. Proven, not guessed.
  • Orion validates our defences: it puts up the compensating control, the shield, then tests it. The shield holds, and the test sets off our detection back home. Controls and detections, both validated.
  • The attackers show up, and bounce off the shield. Blocked in ninety seconds.
  • Then remediation and patching: repair agents patch each hole, and the fix rolls out to all two hundred and thirty, verified.
  • Case closed. All of it, map, prove, validate, fix, within one hour. Read the log top to bottom: different agents, one case, one loop.
